title: How Dreadlocks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how dreadlocks form and their history. They cover prehistoric and ancient dreads (Peruvian mummies, Aztec priests), religious groups that wear dreads (Coptic priests in Ethiopia, Sadhu sect of Hinduism honoring Shiva, Rastafarians), and Bob Marley's role in spreading dreads and Rastafarianism to the West. They discuss the possible Mau Mau origin of the name, anti-dreadlock sentiment, and step-by-step DIY dreading (washing, sectioning, product like wax or aloe, clockwise twisting, backcombing for straight hair, the locking stage, palm rolling, maintenance, mildew prevention, sleeping protection, removing dreads). They close with myths and truths (Samson, ancient Celts and Egyptians, bullet-proofing, charity donation, workplace firing) and a listener mail segment about encouragement for a 15-year-old, plus a plug for the It Gets Better Project.

segments.title: Opening banter and the hippie dreadlock mystery
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about Chuck being under the weather, then Josh recounts hippie-era curiosity about how to dread hair and a friend whose greasy hair kept it from tangling.

segments.title: Ancient and religious dreadlocks
segments.summary: The hosts discuss prehistoric dreads from neglect, a theory about leaves and dirt absorbing grease, Peruvian mummies and Aztec priests with dreads, and religious groups such as Coptic priests in Ethiopia and the Sadhu sect of Hinduism.

segments.title: Rastafarianism, Bob Marley, and the Mau Mau
segments.summary: Dreads are linked to Rastafarianism, which grew from belief in Haile Selassie I as Messiah and rebelled against European beauty ideals. Bob Marley popularized dreads in the West. The name may derive from the Mau Mau uprising against British colonial rule in Kenya, which may have inspired dread in British soldiers.

segments.title: Anti-dreadlock backlash and media portrayals
segments.summary: Bob Marley's popularity in the 1970s also fueled anti-dreadlock sentiment, tied to drug use. Movies Marked for Death and Predator 2 depicted menacing dreadlocked gangs.

segments.title: How to start dreadlocks step by step
segments.summary: Steps include washing with a natural shampoo and drying, sectioning hair into squares (larger squares make bigger dreads), adding product (purists use only water, others use wax or aloe cream), and twisting clockwise so the direction is remembered.

segments.title: Backcombing, locticians, and the locking stage
segments.summary: For straight hair, backcombing with a fine metal comb tangles the hair to jump-start dreads. Locticians can create faster dreads but may look fake. Dreads take months to a year, passing through budding and locking stages, with space left near the scalp so hair can grow.

segments.title: Maintenance, mildew, sleeping, and removing dreads
segments.summary: Palm rolling maintains tangles; dreads need regular waxing, washing with tea tree oil soap, wringing and thorough blow drying to prevent mildew. Sleeping with a bandana or pillowcase protects them. Removing dreads takes a lot of work, and shaving may be needed.

segments.title: Myths and truths about dreadlocks
segments.summary: Myths covered include Samson's dreads, ancient Celts and Egyptians wearing dreads, dreads stopping bullets, and dreads being donated to charity. Dreadlocked employees can be fired, though Rastafarians may have legal recourse.

segments.title: Listener mail from Eddie and It Gets Better
segments.summary: Eddie, a fifteen-year-old, thanks the hosts for encouragement about high school. The hosts plug the It Gets Better Project founded by Dan Savage.
